summary: Short answer to the owner: yes, payers almost always have to answer, on a clock, and the law already attaches real consequences to silence or to a defective denial. The lawful 'teeth' are those consequences stated as plain facts, not threats. To beat an automated denial, make the payer prove that a qualified person applied published criteria to this patient's own record; most rules below exist to force exactly that. (1) Make them show their work: Medicare Advantage denials must state specific reasons (42 CFR 422.568(e)) and an adverse medical-necessity decision must be reviewed by a physician or other qualified clinician before it issues (422.566(d)); internal criteria must be public with an evidence summary (422.101(b)(6)); CMS says an algorithm may assist but may not decide coverage on a larger data set instead of the patient's own record (Feb. 6, 2024 FAQ). ERISA and ACA plans must give the claim file, internal policies and the identity of the experts consulted, free, and must apply plan terms consistently (29 CFR 2560.503-1); a plan that does not strictly follow the rules loses its internal appeal process (deemed exhaustion). Kentucky requires same or similar specialty physicians for medical-necessity denials and reviewer license numbers on prior-approval denial notices (KRS 304.17A-607); Indiana requires a same-specialty clinical peer who owes the patient a duty of care, deems late prior-authorization decisions approved (IC 27-1-37.5), and from 2026 bars insurers from using AI as the sole basis for a medical-necessity downcode, requires AI disclosure, and must accept downcode appeals in batches 'without restriction' (IC 27-1-52). (2) Use the payer's own words and data: plan documents that promise clinicians decide are enforceable contract terms (Lokken v. UnitedHealth, D. Minn. 2025; Barrows v. Humana, W.D. Ky. 2025); payers publish their own negotiated rates (Transparency in Coverage files); prior payments of the same service are evidence of consistent application, and statutory lookback limits (KY 24 months, IN 180 days for recoupment in 2027 plan years, Medicare 1 and 4 years) cap the risk that citing them invites a takeback. (3) Silence escalates automatically: an MA reconsideration not decided in 60 days is an affirmation that must go to the CMS independent review entity (422.590(d)), and Star Ratings count how often that entity overturns the plan, including non-contract provider appeals; Medicaid plans that miss notice or timing rules lose their appeal step (438.408(c)(3)); Kentucky interest is added without any demand (KRS 304.17A-730). (4) Pattern evidence moves regulators: Kentucky insurers must answer the Department within 15 days and the commissioner must make a finding and weigh complaints at renewal, and prompt-pay violations carry fines of $1,000 a day or 10% of the claim; Indiana insurers must give a written report with specific reasons within 20 business days of a complaint, and repeated unfair practices carry penalties of up to $25,000 ($50,000 if knowing) per act; CMS requires MA plans to resolve tracked complaints within 30 days. For 60-cent items, the cheapest lawful channels are: Kentucky payment-error notices (no appeal required, 30 days to correct), Medicare clerical-error reopenings (no deadline), Indiana batch downcode appeals, payer bulk tools (UHC Claims Research Project, Cigna multi-patient fee disputes), Kentucky Medicaid bundled external review of a policy or practice, and one pattern complaint per payer per issue. What not to do: never threaten criminal charges, licensing complaints against a reviewer, publicity or a group boycott, or offer to give or withhold information in someone else's lawsuit in exchange for payment (KRS 514.080; IC 35-45-2-1; SCR 3.130(3.4)(f) for lawyers); never state a fact that is not true or add to a note after the fact except as a dated, signed late entry (18 U.S.C. 1035; KRS 304.47-020; PIM 3.3.2.5); keep a person's review on every claim an automated tool submits (required in Indiana, IC 27-1-52-9(b)); and return Medicare and Medicaid overpayments the same review uncovers within 60 days of identifying them. Real risks: insurers must run fraud units, may audit within statutory windows, and MA plans may end a contract without cause on 60 days' notice; anti-retaliation protection for providers is narrow (expedited MA requests, Medicaid appeal support, anti-gag clauses). State law does not reach MA plans (422.402) or self-funded ERISA plans; for those, federal rules and the contract govern.

rules.applies_to: Medicare Advantage plans (Humana MA, Anthem MA, UHC MA, WellCare MA and others) when they deny payment in whole or in part; notice goes to the enrollee and the physician or provider involved, as appropriate. Not applicable integrated plans (they follow 422.629 to 422.634).
rules.requires: A written denial notice in approved language that states the specific reasons for the denial and describes the reconsideration process; a late notice is itself an appealable denial.
rules.deadline: Payment decisions follow 422.520 timing (non-contracted clean claims 30 days, other non-contracted claims 60 days); see the medicare_advantage area for the full clock.
rules.consequence: A bare remark code or silence does not satisfy the rule; missing the deadline converts silence into an adverse organization determination that opens reconsideration and, if upheld, the CMS independent review entity.
rules.provider_use: When an MA plan pays short with only a CARC or says nothing, cite 422.568(e)(2) and ask for the specific reason in writing. For non-contracted claims, treat silence past the deadline as a denial (422.568(f)) and file a reconsideration with a waiver of liability. For contracted claims where the patient owes nothing, use the contract dispute process (422.562(c)(2)); the specific-reasons rule still supports the demand for an explanation.
rules.quote: (2) State the specific reasons for the denial; ... this failure itself constitutes an adverse organization determination and may be appealed.

rules.applies_to: Medicare Advantage plans, any partially or fully adverse medical-necessity organization determination, including refusal to pay after the service (CMS FAQ of Feb. 6, 2024, Q9 treats payment refusals as organization determinations under 422.566(b)(3)).
rules.requires: A licensed physician or other appropriate clinician with expertise in the relevant field, who knows Medicare coverage criteria, must review before the denial issues. Same specialty is not required in every case.
rules.consequence: A medical-necessity denial issued without that review is noncompliant; argue it on reconsideration and at the independent review entity; report a pattern to CMS.
rules.provider_use: In every MA medical-necessity appeal, ask the plan to state who reviewed the denial before it issued and in what field (for Mohs, radiation or pathology, a dermatologist or radiation oncologist matters). If the file shows only an automated edit, say so and cite 422.566(d).
rules.quote: the organization determination must be reviewed by a physician or other appropriate health care professional with expertise in the field of medicine or health care that is appropriate for the services at issue, including knowledge of Medicare coverage criteria, before the MA organization issues the organization determination decision.

rules.applies_to: Medicare Advantage plans, basic (Part A and B) benefits.
rules.requires: Medicare's own criteria (statute, regulation, NCD, LCD) control; a plan may use internal criteria only where Medicare's are not fully established, and must publish them with a summary of the evidence.
rules.consequence: A denial that rests on unpublished criteria, or on criteria stricter than a governing LCD, is noncompliant and should be overturned on reconsideration or by the independent review entity.
rules.provider_use: Cite the CGS (Kentucky) or WPS (Indiana) LCD for the service and demand the exact publicly posted internal criterion and evidence summary if the plan relied on anything else.
rules.quote: MA organizations may create publicly accessible internal coverage criteria that are based on current evidence in widely used treatment guidelines or clinical literature when coverage criteria are not fully established in applicable Medicare statutes, regulations, NCDs or LCDs. ... (A) The internal coverage criteria in use and a summary of evidence that was considered during the development of the internal coverage criteria used to make medical necessity determinations;

rules.citation: CMS HPMS memo, Frequently Asked Questions related to Coverage Criteria and Utilization Management Requirements in CMS Final Rule (CMS-4201-F), Feb. 6, 2024, Question 2
rules.applies_to: Medicare Advantage organizations and Medicare-Medicaid plans (CMS guidance interpreting 42 CFR 422.101(c), not itself a regulation).
rules.requires: Algorithms may assist, but each medical-necessity decision must rest on the individual patient's history, the physician's recommendations and the clinical notes, under published criteria that AI may not shift.
rules.consequence: A denial produced by a model rather than an individualized review is noncompliant with 422.101(c); CMS enforces through audits and compliance actions.
rules.provider_use: The core 'AI against AI' paragraph: ask whether an algorithm, predictive tool or automated edit was used, which documents in this patient's record the reviewer read, and which published criterion applied. Quote the FAQ.
rules.quote: an algorithm that determines coverage based on a larger data set instead of the individual patient's medical history, the physician's recommendations, or clinical notes would not be compliant with § 422.101(c). ... Because publicly posted coverage criteria are static and unchanging, artificial intelligence cannot be used to shift the coverage criteria over time.

rules.applies_to: Medicare Advantage payment reconsiderations by enrollees, their representatives and non-contracted providers who sign a waiver of liability. Not contracted-provider payment disputes where the enrollee has no further liability (422.562(c)(2)); those follow the contract.
rules.requires: Decide a payment reconsideration within 60 calendar days; if the plan upholds any part, or misses the deadline, it must send the file to the CMS independent review entity itself.
rules.deadline: 60 calendar days from receipt of the reconsideration request.
rules.consequence: Silence is an affirmation and the case goes to independent review automatically; overturns there count against the plan's Star Ratings (TR-06).
rules.provider_use: State the clock and the automatic forwarding in the letter as a fact. Track day 60 for every non-contracted reconsideration and check the independent review entity's status lookup if the plan has not forwarded the case.
rules.quote: If the MA organization affirms, in whole or in part, its adverse organization determination, it must prepare a written explanation and send the case file to the independent entity contracted by CMS no later than 60 calendar days from the date it receives the request for a standard reconsideration. ... this failure constitutes an affirmation of its adverse organization determination, and the MA organization must submit the file to the independent entity ... the claim payment determination is not subject to the appeal process in this subpart.

rules.citation: CMS 2027 Star Ratings Technical Notes, measure C31 Reviewing Appeals Decisions
rules.applies_to: Medicare Advantage contracts (Part C Star Ratings).
rules.requires: Nothing of the provider; it measures the share of the plan's appeals that the independent review entity upheld.
rules.consequence: Every overturn at the independent review entity lowers the plan's score on a measure (weight 2, per the medicare_advantage area) that CMS uses in Star Ratings.
rules.provider_use: Leverage is real but should be stated factually, for example: 'If this denial is upheld, federal rules require you to forward it to the independent review entity.' Do not threaten ratings; the rule does the work.
rules.quote: This rating shows how often an independent reviewer found the health plan's decision to deny coverage to be reasonable. ... This includes appeals requested by a beneficiary, appeals requested by a party on behalf of a beneficiary, and appeals requested by non-contract providers.

rules.applies_to: Medicare Advantage plans, complaints logged in CMS's Complaints Tracking Module, including provider complaints submitted through CMS's online provider complaint form (see medicare_advantage area).
rules.requires: Resolve a tracked complaint within 30 calendar days of assignment and attempt contact within 7.
rules.deadline: 30 calendar days from CMS assignment (2 or 7 days for immediate or urgent beneficiary access cases).
rules.consequence: A regulatory clock on the plan, and the complaint is visible to CMS account managers; complaint counts feed a Star Ratings measure (per medicare_advantage area).
rules.provider_use: Use one complaint per payer per pattern (late payment, ignored reconsiderations, missing interest), with counts and dollars and no patient identifiers beyond what CMS asks for.
rules.quote: The MA organization must resolve all other complaints within 30 calendar days of the assignment date. ... the MA organization must attempt to contact the individual who filed a complaint within 7 calendar days of the assignment date.

rules.applies_to: ERISA employee benefit plans, self-funded and insured (plans administered by UMR, UHC, Anthem, Cigna; the UMWA Funds are ERISA plans per the erisa_commercial area). The provider acts as the claimant's authorized representative under the plan's procedures (2560.503-1(b)(4)).
rules.requires: Free copies of everything relied on, submitted, considered or generated, the documents showing consistency safeguards, and any internal policy or guidance about the denied service, whether or not relied on.
rules.deadline: The regulation sets no day count for producing documents; the appeal itself must be decided within the post-service timelines (60 days for one level).
rules.consequence: Not providing them is a failure to follow reasonable claims procedures, so the claim is deemed exhausted and may go to external review or court (2560.503-1(l)).
rules.provider_use: With a signed authorized-representative form, ask for the full claim file including any automated edit, scoring output or reviewer notes and the payment policy for the code. What comes back shows whether a person or a rule engine decided.
rules.quote: a claimant shall be provided, upon request and free of charge, reasonable access to, and copies of, all documents, records, and other information relevant to the claimant's claim for benefits. ... constitutes a statement of policy or guidance with respect to the plan concerning the denied treatment option or benefit for the claimant's diagnosis, without regard to whether such advice or statement was relied upon in making the benefit determination.

rules.applies_to: ERISA plans, self-funded and insured.
rules.requires: Safeguards ensuring plan terms are applied consistently to similarly situated claimants, and production of the documents showing those safeguards on request.
rules.consequence: Inconsistent application without explanation supports reversal on appeal or in court; failure to produce the safeguard documents is a procedural failure (deemed exhaustion).
rules.provider_use: Turn the payer's own payment history into precedent: state, in de-identified aggregate form, that the same plan paid the same code, modifier and diagnosis pairing N times between two dates at $X, and demand the consistency documents. Do not list other patients' names or member numbers (HIPAA minimum necessary, TR-56).
rules.quote: where appropriate, the plan provisions have been applied consistently with respect to similarly situated claimants. ... Demonstrates compliance with the administrative processes and safeguards required pursuant to paragraph (b)(5) of this section in making the benefit determination

rules.applies_to: Group health plans subject to ERISA (self-funded and insured).
rules.requires: Appeals of medical-judgment denials must be decided after consulting a clinician trained in the relevant field, and the plan must identify the experts it consulted.
rules.consequence: Without that consultation the review is not 'full and fair'; deemed exhaustion and court review follow.
rules.provider_use: Ask for the name and specialty of the clinician consulted on appeal. For a Mohs, radiation or dermatopathology denial, a reviewer outside the field is a procedural defect worth naming.
rules.quote: the appropriate named fiduciary shall consult with a health care professional who has appropriate training and experience in the field of medicine involved in the medical judgment ... Provide for the identification of medical or vocational experts whose advice was obtained on behalf of the plan in connection with a claimant's adverse benefit determination, without regard to whether the advice was relied upon in making the benefit determination

rules.applies_to: Non-grandfathered group health plans (including self-funded ERISA plans) and health insurance issuers; the claimant includes an authorized representative.
rules.requires: Strict adherence to every internal claims and appeals requirement, including notice content and timing.
rules.consequence: The claimant may go straight to external review or to court under ERISA 502(a) or state law; the de minimis excuse is lost when violations are a pattern or practice.
rules.provider_use: Log every defect per payer (missing denial-code meaning, no plan standard cited, late decision). A logged pattern defeats the de minimis defense and supports skipping the plan's second appeal level.
rules.quote: In the case of a plan or issuer that fails to strictly adhere to all the requirements of this paragraph (b)(2) with respect to a claim, the claimant is deemed to have exhausted the internal claims and appeals process of this paragraph (b) ... This exception is not available if the violation is part of a pattern or practice of violations by the plan or issuer.

rules.applies_to: Kentucky insurers and private review agents (fully insured plans, HMOs, self-insured governmental and church plans per KRS 304.17A-005(29), and Medicaid MCOs through KRS 205.522, per the kentucky area). Not self-funded ERISA plans; not Medicare Advantage (42 CFR 422.402). The license-number notice rule covers denials of items that require prior approval.
rules.requires: Medical-necessity and experimental denials (prospective or retrospective) made only by licensed physicians of the same or similar specialty when possible; notices with specific medical and scientific reasons, the reviewer's title and, to a provider, the reviewer's license number.
rules.deadline: Urgent decisions 24 hours and nonurgent 5 days after the necessary information (KRS 304.17A-607(2)(i)).
rules.consequence: A late utilization review decision is deemed a prior authorization; a denial by a non-physician or without the required notice content is a ground for appeal and a DOI utilization review complaint.
rules.provider_use: Ask for the reviewing physician's specialty and license number and compare to the ordering dermatologist; a nurse or a generalist denial of Mohs or radiation is contestable on its face.
rules.quote: only licensed physicians, who are of the same or similar specialty and subspecialty, when possible, as the ordering provider, shall: ... The title of the reviewer making the decision, except that a written notice provided to a provider shall also include, if applicable, the medical license number of the reviewer making the decision; ... failure to make a determination and provide written notice within the time frames set forth in this section shall be deemed to be a prior authorization for the health care services or benefits subject to the review.

rules.applies_to: Utilization review entities performing prior authorization for Indiana health plans: accident and sickness policies, HMOs, Medicaid risk-based managed care and the state employee self-insurance program (IC 27-1-37.5-5). Self-funded ERISA plans likely preempted; not Medicare Advantage.
rules.requires: Every adverse medical-necessity determination and every appeal decided by a clinical peer (same ABMS or AOA specialty, and same subspecialty when the review concerns subspecialty care) under an Indiana-licensed medical director.
rules.consequence: Missed deadlines or requirements make the service automatically authorized; the clinical peer owes the patient a duty of care.
rules.provider_use: For Indiana prior-authorization denials, demand the peer's board certification; a non-dermatologist denial of a dermatology request does not meet the statute. Cite automatic authorization when a deadline was missed.
rules.quote: adverse determinations based on medical necessity are made; and (B) appeals are reviewed and decided; by a clinical peer ... is certified in the same specialty as the physician under review ... owes a duty to the covered individual to exercise the applicable standard of care. ... the health care service subject to prior authorization shall be automatically deemed authorized by the utilization review entity.

rules.applies_to: Indiana accident and sickness insurers, HMOs and their third-party contractors (IC 27-1-52-5, -6). Not Medicaid or Medicaid MCOs (27-1-52-0.3); not self-funded ERISA plans; not Medicare Advantage.
rules.requires: No automated or AI tool as the sole basis for a medical-necessity downcode without a person reviewing the record; disclosure when AI is used to downcode or deny prior authorization; no downcode on the diagnosis code alone; a downcode notice with CARC and RARC, the specific reason and clinical criteria, original and revised codes and amounts, and appeal rights.
rules.consequence: A downcode without these is contrary to statute; Department of Insurance rules are to follow (27-1-52-14). Penalty provisions were not found in the chapter itself (see open questions).
rules.provider_use: RemitWatch already detects downcodes: for Indiana fully insured payers, every downcode without the required notice elements, or made on diagnosis alone, is a ready-made appeal point. Ask whether AI was used and whether a person read the record.
rules.quote: as the sole basis to downcode a claim based on medical necessity without the review of the covered individual's medical record by an employee or contractor of the insurer. ... An insurer must disclose in an easily accessible and readable manner when artificial intelligence is used to: ... An insurer may not downcode a claim based solely on the reported diagnosis code. ... the specific reason for the downcoding, including reference to the clinical criteria used to justify the downcoding;

rules.applies_to: Same scope as TR-14 (Indiana fully insured and HMO; not Medicaid).
rules.requires: Accept batch appeals of similar downcodes without restriction; allow at least 180 days to appeal; give a named contact for the appeal.
rules.deadline: Appeal window of at least 180 days (the insurer's own timeline may be longer).
rules.consequence: Refusing a batch appeal violates the statute (complaint to the Indiana Department of Insurance).
rules.provider_use: The legal basis for one letter covering every similar downcode for a payer; this is what makes small downcodes worth chasing.
rules.quote: An insurer shall allow a provider to appeal in batches of similar claims involving substantially similar downcoding issues without restriction. ... a timeline for submission of an appeal that is not less than one hundred eighty (180) days.

rules.applies_to: Indiana accident and sickness insurers (including PPO plans and claims administrators that settle claims, IC 27-8-5.7-3) and HMOs. Not self-funded ERISA plans; not Medicare Advantage.
rules.requires: No recoding to a lower-paying CPT code unless the billed code breaks coding rules, clinical guidelines or the contract, or a person reviewed the medical record.
rules.consequence: An unsupported recode is contrary to statute; the section expressly preserves the provider's appeal.
rules.provider_use: Ask which coding rule the billed code broke or who reviewed the record; with neither, the recode fails.
rules.quote: An insurer may not alter the CPT code submitted for a clean claim or pay for a CPT code of lesser monetary value unless: ... the medical record of the clean claim has been reviewed by an employee or contractor of the insurer.

rules.applies_to: Kentucky and Indiana Medicaid managed care plans (Humana, Anthem, WellCare, Aetna Better Health, Passport, MHS, CareSource and others), enrollee appeals of adverse benefit determinations.
rules.requires: Notices must explain the enrollee's right to free copies of everything relevant, including medical necessity criteria; decisions on medical-necessity appeals by people with appropriate clinical expertise; standard appeal resolution within 30 calendar days (plus up to 14).
rules.deadline: Appeal within 60 calendar days of the notice; plan decides within 30 calendar days.
rules.consequence: Missing the notice or timing rules means the appeal is deemed exhausted and the state fair hearing opens.
rules.provider_use: With the patient's written consent, appeal on the patient's behalf and ask for the criteria free of charge. Provider-own payment disputes follow the state's provider dispute rules (TR-18, TR-19, TR-42).
rules.quote: Such information includes medical necessity criteria, and any processes, strategies, or evidentiary standards used in setting coverage limits. ... If State law permits and with the written consent of the enrollee, a provider or an authorized representative may request an appeal or file a grievance, or request a State fair hearing, on behalf of an enrollee. ... the enrollee is deemed to have exhausted the MCO's, PIHP's, or PAHP's appeals process.

rules.applies_to: Kentucky Medicaid managed care organizations (all KY MCOs).
rules.requires: On any adverse payment or coverage determination: all relevant documents and criteria at no cost to the provider, and a written reply giving all reasons. Authorization decisions must be consistent with comparable members and with previous affirmative coverage decisions.
rules.consequence: Contract sanctions by the Department for Medicaid Services (KRS 205.534(6), per the kentucky area); support for internal appeal and external independent review.
rules.provider_use: Ask for the criteria and every reason in writing on each adverse decision; for authorizations, cite the plan's own prior approvals of the same service as required consistency (2)(b).
rules.quote: copies of all documents, records, and other information relevant to a determination, including medical necessity criteria and any processes, strategies, or evidentiary standards relied upon, if requested by the provider. ... a written reply in sufficient detail to inform the provider of all reasons for the determination. ... Medicaid members with comparable medical needs receive a comparable, consistent level, amount, and duration of services as supported by the member's medical condition, records, and previous affirmative coverage decisions.

rules.applies_to: Kentucky Medicaid managed care organizations; providers who exhausted the MCO's written internal appeal.
rules.requires: External independent third-party review of the MCO's final decision, with multiple claims bundled when a policy or practice is alleged; an in-person meeting on request for clean claims unpaid in violation of prompt pay, or claims unpaid 45 days or more that exceed $2,500 alone or together.
rules.deadline: Request external review within 60 calendar days of the final internal decision (907 KAR 17:035, per the kentucky area).
rules.consequence: Binding review, appealable to an administrative hearing; the loser pays the hearing fee (per the kentucky area).
rules.provider_use: The Kentucky Medicaid batch lever: one review for every claim hit by the same MCO policy, and an in-person meeting once small unpaid claims add up past $2,500.
rules.quote: A provider may submit multiple claims to be appealed in a single external independent third-party review if the provider alleges that a Medicaid managed care organization has implemented a policy or practice that results in the denial, in whole or in part, of those claims. ... Any claim that remains unpaid for forty-five (45) days or more after the date the claim is received by the managed care organization and that individually or in the aggregate exceeds two thousand five hundred dollars ($2,500);

rules.citation: Kisting-Leung v. Cigna Corp., No. 2:23-cv-01477-DAD-CSK (E.D. Cal.), Order of Mar. 30, 2025 (Doc. 55, filed Mar. 31, 2025), quoting Cigna's declaration (Doc. 46-14 at para. 13)
rules.applies_to: Cigna commercial plans (insured and administrative-services-only).
rules.requires: Nothing by itself; it is Cigna's sworn description of its own practice, recited by the court.
rules.consequence: If a Cigna denial looks automated and no separate PxDx letter arrived, Cigna's own statement says one should have.
rules.provider_use: On Cigna denials, ask whether PxDx or any automated review was used and request the PxDx letter and the named clinical coverage policy.
rules.quote: if a claim was denied based on PxDx review, both the patient and healthcare provider will receive a separate letter detailing the services billed, the diagnosis codes billed, and the applicable Cigna clinical coverage policy used in adjudicating that PxDx denial.

rules.applies_to: Non-grandfathered group health plans (including self-funded) and group health insurance issuers. Not Medicare Advantage, Medicaid or VA.
rules.requires: Monthly public in-network rate files with each negotiated rate in dollars, tied to the provider's NPI, TIN and place of service.
rules.consequence: The payer's own published rate is evidence of what it agreed to pay.
rules.provider_use: Compute the expected allowed amount for every commercial line from the payer's own file and cite the file date in underpayment disputes. This replaces contract look-ups and lets small underpayments be proven at scale.
rules.quote: Reflected as dollar amounts, with respect to each covered item or service that is furnished by an in-network provider. ... Associated with the National Provider Identifier (NPI), Tax Identification Number (TIN), and Place of Service Code for each in-network provider; ... The machine-readable files must be publicly available and accessible to any person free of charge and without conditions ... this section does not apply to grandfathered health plans.

rules.applies_to: Kentucky insurers under KRS 304.17A (fully insured, HMOs, governmental and church self-insured plans; Medicaid MCOs through KRS 205.593). Not self-funded ERISA; not Medicare Advantage.
rules.requires: Retroactive denials only within 24 months of payment (fraud excepted); provider correction requests within 24 months of receiving payment.
rules.deadline: 24 months both ways.
rules.consequence: Older payments cannot be taken back (absent fraud), so citing them as precedent carries no recoupment risk; the provider loses correction rights after 24 months.
rules.provider_use: Cite prior payments older than 24 months freely as precedent; file every Kentucky underpayment notice well inside 24 months of the payment date.
rules.quote: Except in cases of fraud, an insurer may only retroactively deny reimbursement to a provider during the twenty-four (24) month period after the date that the insurer paid the claim submitted by the provider. ... An insurer shall not be required to correct a payment error to a provider if the provider's request for a payment correction is filed more than twenty-four (24) months after the date that the provider received payment for the claim from the insurer.

rules.applies_to: Indiana accident and sickness insurers for policies issued, delivered, amended or renewed after June 30, 2026 that cover plan years beginning after Dec. 31, 2026 (IC 27-8-5.7-0.5). Earlier policies: the 2025 text allowed two years each way. Fraud found by a court excepted.
rules.requires: Recoupment and overpayment requests within 180 days of payment; audits within 3 years; provider notice of a payment error within 180 days of receiving payment.
rules.deadline: 180 days from receipt of payment for the provider's payment-error notice (2027 plan years onward).
rules.consequence: A late underpayment notice is lost; a late recoupment is barred.
rules.provider_use: Put a hard 180-day clock on every Indiana fully insured underpayment from the 835 payment date; batch notices weekly so none age out.
rules.quote: An insurer may not recoup a paid claim more than one hundred eighty (180) days after the date on which the claim was initially paid. ... An insurer may not retroactively audit a paid claim more than three (3) years after the date on which the claim was initially paid. ... An insurer may not be required to correct a payment error to a provider if notice of the payment error is not provided within one hundred eighty (180) days after payment for a fully adjudicated claim is received.

rules.applies_to: Traditional Medicare (CGS for Kentucky, WPS for Indiana) and, through 422.616, Medicare Advantage determinations.
rules.requires: Contractor-initiated reopenings: any reason within 1 year, good cause within 4 years, fraud at any time. A party may ask at any time to fix a clerical error behind an unfavorable determination.
rules.deadline: None for clerical-error reopenings requested by the party.
rules.consequence: Old paid claims are safe from reopening absent good cause or fraud; clerical errors never time out.
rules.provider_use: For small-dollar Medicare errors caused by keying or data mistakes, a reopening request is the cheapest lawful channel and has no deadline. Payments older than 4 years can be cited as precedent without reopening risk unless fraud is alleged.
rules.quote: Within 1 year from the date of the initial determination or redetermination for any reason. ... Within 4 years from the date of the initial determination or redetermination for good cause as defined in § 405.986. ... A party may request that a contractor reopen its initial determination at any time if the initial determination is unfavorable, in whole or in part, to the party thereto, but only for the purpose of correcting a clerical error on which that determination was based. ... may be reopened and revised by the entity that made the determination or decision, under the rules in part 405 of this chapter.

rules.applies_to: Kentucky insurers under KRS 304.17A, including Medicaid MCOs through KRS 205.593; contracted providers paid below the contracted rate.
rules.requires: No appeal for contract-rate payment errors; correct and pay within 30 calendar days of documentation.
rules.deadline: Insurer: 30 calendar days from receipt of the documentation. Provider: within 24 months of payment (TR-22).
rules.consequence: Failure to correct is a prompt-pay violation subject to KRS 304.99-123 fines; knowing and willful failure is an unfair claims settlement practice (KRS 304.12-230(17), per the kentucky area). No interest accrues on the correction itself.
rules.provider_use: The cheapest lawful channel for small Kentucky underpayments: one documented payment-error notice per payer listing every underpaid line (code, date, contracted amount, paid amount, difference). No appeal form is needed by law.
rules.quote: An insurer shall not require a provider to appeal errors in payment where the insurer has not paid the claim according to the contracted rate. Miscalculations in payments made by the insurer shall be corrected and paid within thirty (30) calendar days upon the insurer's receipt of documentation from the provider verifying the error. ... An insurer shall not be required to pay interest on corrected payments made in accordance with KRS 304.17A-708(1).

rules.applies_to: Kentucky insurers under KRS 304.17A (and Medicaid MCOs through KRS 205.593) on clean claims paid after the 30-day deadline in KRS 304.17A-702.
rules.requires: Interest added automatically, without a demand, at 12%, 18% or 21% a year depending on lateness (rates per the kentucky area), paid within 30 days after the claim is paid.
rules.deadline: Interest due within 30 days after payment of the late claim.
rules.consequence: Unpaid interest is itself a prompt-pay violation (KRS 304.99-123 fines).
rules.provider_use: No demand letter is legally needed: compute expected interest from the receipt date on each late clean claim and list missing interest in the payer's quarterly pattern complaint.
rules.quote: the insurer shall add the interest payable to the amount of the unpaid claim without the necessity for any claim for that interest to be made by the provider filing the original claim. ... shall pay the interest required by KRS 304.17A-730 within thirty (30) days after the date a claim is paid.

rules.applies_to: Kentucky claims 'arising under the terms of any contract of insurance' (fully insured). Not self-funded ERISA plans; not Medicare Advantage. Interplay with the health-specific prompt pay statutes is not confirmed (open question).
rules.requires: Payment within 30 days of notice and proof of claim.
rules.consequence: Attorney's fees to the health care provider when the delay lacked reasonable foundation; 12% interest on the final settlement when the insurer made no good-faith attempt to settle (304.12-235(2)).
rules.provider_use: Fee shifting is what makes suing over small Kentucky fully insured claims rational; mention it as a fact in a final notice before filing.
rules.quote: the delay was without reasonable foundation, the insured person or health care provider shall be entitled to be reimbursed for his reasonable attorney's fees incurred.

rules.applies_to: Kentucky insurers under the prompt pay statutes, and Medicaid MCOs (304.99-123(3) per the kentucky area).
rules.requires: Compliance with KRS 304.17A-700 to -730; the per-day fine has a safe harbor when 95% of clean claims (and 90% of dollars) are timely in the quarter.
rules.consequence: Department fines of $1,000 a day or 10% of the unpaid claim, whichever is greater, per day; up to $10,000 for willful violations or a pattern.
rules.provider_use: Pattern evidence matters: report late and unpaid clean claims per payer per quarter with counts and percentages, which is how the safe harbor is measured.
rules.quote: A fine of one thousand dollars ($1,000) per day or ten percent (10%) of the unpaid claim amount, whichever is greater, for each day that a clean claim remains unpaid ... has a pattern of repeated violations of KRS 304.17A-700 to 304.17A-730

rules.applies_to: Anyone in the business of insurance in Kentucky (insurers, HMOs, administrators); complaints may be filed by providers.
rules.requires: The insurer answers the Department in 15 calendar days; the commissioner makes a finding to both sides; complaints are recorded, kept 5 years, indexed by insurer and weighed at license renewal.
rules.deadline: 15 calendar days for the insurer's response.
rules.consequence: A recorded finding, an enforcement record and renewal consequences.
rules.provider_use: A written complaint forces a written answer on a short clock; file per payer per pattern with the dollar total and representative examples.
rules.quote: the entity or individual shall send a written or electronic message response to the commissioner within fifteen (15) calendar days from the date of the commissioner's letter. ... Upon review of a complaint, the commissioner shall make a finding to the entity or individual and the complainant. ... The commissioner shall consider complaints received by the department before issuing or renewing any certificate of authority or license.

rules.applies_to: Kentucky insurers, including agents and third-party administrators (806 KAR 12:092 Section 1(9), per the kentucky area). Not Medicare Advantage; self-funded ERISA plans are generally outside state insurance regulation.
rules.requires: Prompt acknowledgment and action on claim communications; a reasonable explanation of the basis for any denial; the Department's guidance standard is 15 calendar days to answer any written communication about a claim.
rules.deadline: 15 calendar days (regulatory guidance standard).
rules.consequence: Unfair claims settlement practice: Department enforcement (desist orders, fines, license action). The regulation states it guides the commissioner; private suits by providers are an open question.
rules.provider_use: Answers 'must they answer?' for Kentucky fully insured payers: any written communication about a claim starts a 15-day response standard. Cite it on day 16 in the complaint.
rules.quote: Failing to acknowledge and act reasonably promptly upon communications with respect to claims arising under insurance policies; ... Failing to promptly provide a reasonable explanation of the basis in the insurance policy in relation to the facts or applicable law for denial of a claim or for the offer of a compromise settlement; ... The insurer shall acknowledge and respond within fifteen (15) calendar days to any written communications relating to a claim.

rules.applies_to: Indiana insurers. The complaint right belongs to 'a person who has submitted a claim to an insurer', which covers a provider that submitted the claim. Not Medicare Advantage; not self-funded ERISA plans.
rules.requires: If the commissioner believes an unfair practice occurred, the complaint goes to the insurer within 10 business days; the insurer must then investigate and give the commissioner and the complaining party a written report with specific reasons for action and inaction and a good-faith settlement estimate.
rules.deadline: Insurer's written report: 20 business days from receipt of the complaint.
rules.consequence: Unfair practices committed with such frequency as to indicate a general practice are unfair or deceptive acts; after a hearing, civil penalties up to $25,000 per act ($50,000 if knowing) and license action.
rules.provider_use: Indiana's strongest 'must answer' tool: a complaint yields a written report with specific reasons in 20 business days. Pattern evidence (counts, dates, dollars) meets the general-practice standard.
rules.quote: believes that an unfair claim settlement practice described in section 4.5 of this chapter has been committed in connection with the claim; ... Within twenty (20) business days from the date of receipt of the complaint, the insurer shall provide to the commissioner and the complaining party a written report ... Committing or performing, with such frequency as to indicate a general practice, unfair claim settlement practices ... Payment of a civil penalty of not more than twenty-five thousand dollars ($25,000) for each act or violation.

rules.applies_to: Indiana accident and sickness insurers (HMOs under IC 27-13-36.2). Not self-funded ERISA; not Medicare Advantage.
rules.requires: Pay or deny a clean claim within 30 days (electronic) or 45 days (paper); interest from day 31 or 46 until paid at the rate set by reference (the Department's bulletins publish it, per the indiana area).
rules.deadline: 30 days electronic, 45 days paper.
rules.consequence: Interest to the provider; aggregate civil penalties by the share of clean claims paid on time ($10,000 to $200,000 tiers).
rules.provider_use: Compute owed interest on every late Indiana clean claim and list it in the payer's pattern complaint; the penalty is measured on the payer's overall on-time rate.
rules.quote: the insurer shall pay the provider that submitted the claim interest on the accident and sickness insurance policy allowable amount of the claim paid under this section. ... In paying interest under subsection (b), an insurer shall use the same interest rate as provided in IC 12-15-21-3(7)(A). ... the commissioner may assess an aggregate civil penalty against the insurer according to the following schedule:

rules.applies_to: Medicare Advantage plans; interest on clean claims applies to non-contracted providers; contracted providers get the prompt-pay terms of their contract.
rules.requires: Non-contracted clean claims: 95% within 30 days with interest at the Medicare rate if late; other non-contracted claims within 60 days.
rules.deadline: 30 days (clean, non-contracted); 60 days (other non-contracted).
rules.consequence: Interest owed; substantial failure to meet prompt payment is a ground for CMS sanctions or termination (422.510(a)(4)(v), per the medicare_advantage area).
rules.provider_use: For out-of-network MA claims, compute the interest owed on late clean claims and request it; for contracted MA plans, quote the contract's prompt-pay clause, which 422.520(b) requires every contract to have.
rules.quote: The MA organization must pay interest on clean claims that are not paid within 30 days in accordance with sections 1816(c)(2)(B) and 1842(c)(2)(B). ... All other claims from non-contracted providers must be paid or denied within 60 calendar days from the date of the request. ... The MA organization is obligated to pay contracted providers under the terms of the contract between the MA organization and the provider.

rules.citation: HHS OIG, OEI-09-18-00260 (April 2022); HHS OIG, OEI-09-16-00410 (September 2018)
rules.applies_to: Medicare Advantage organizations (government audit findings, not law). The 2018 report is at https://oig.hhs.gov/oei/reports/oei-09-16-00410.pdf.
rules.requires: Nothing; evidence.
rules.consequence: Federal findings that a meaningful share of MA payment denials were wrong and that MA plans reversed most appealed denials.
rules.provider_use: Supports a policy of appealing every MA payment denial rather than writing them off, and gives regulators context for a pattern complaint. Cite as context, not as proof about a specific claim.
rules.quote: among the payment requests that MAOs denied, 18 percent met Medicare coverage rules and MAO billing rules. ... This represents a 75 percent success rate ... Most of these overturned denials (82 percent) were for payment to providers for services that the beneficiary already received. ... appealing only 1 percent of denials during

rules.applies_to: Kentucky insurers under KRS 304.17A (not Medicaid MCOs for these sections; not self-funded ERISA; not Medicare Advantage).
rules.requires: Providers may start internal appeals for the patient and, with consent, external review of medical-necessity type adverse determinations; the insurer pays the reviewer (304.17A-625, per the kentucky area).
rules.deadline: External review request within 60 days of the final internal decision (per the kentucky area).
rules.consequence: The independent reviewer's decision binds the insurer; refusing to comply is an unfair claims practice.
rules.provider_use: Collect the patient's written consent early so medical-necessity denials can go to external review without chasing signatures (whether a standing consent signed at intake satisfies the Department's authorization form rules, 806 KAR 17:290, was not confirmed).
rules.quote: The internal appeals process may be initiated by the covered person, an authorized person, or a provider acting on behalf of the covered person. ... A covered person, an authorized person, or a provider acting on behalf of and with the consent of the covered person, may request an external review of an adverse benefit determination, other than a coverage denial, rendered by an insurer, its designee, or agent.

rules.applies_to: Kentucky District Court small claims division, any civil claim within the limit.
rules.requires: Claims of $2,500 or less (interest and costs excluded); no assigned claims or class actions; at most 25 claims a year per party (businesses: per established location in the district open 6 months or more); an affidavit of the count at filing.
rules.consequence: Claims over the count are dismissed at the plaintiff's cost.
rules.provider_use: Small claims is a pressure point, not a scale tool: usable for a handful of fully insured, contract-based disputes a year. Not for claims taken by assignment from patients; Medicare Advantage claims must go through Medicare appeals.
rules.quote: does not exceed two thousand five hundred dollars ($2,500) exclusive of interest and costs. ... No party may file an assigned claim or a class action in the division. ... No party shall file more than twenty-five (25) claims in any one (1) calendar year in the small claims division of any District Court in the Commonwealth.

rules.citation: Indiana Small Claims Rule 8(C) (version effective Jan. 1, 2025)
rules.applies_to: Indiana small claims dockets.
rules.requires: A corporation or LLC may appear through counsel, an owner or a designated full-time employee with a certificate of compliance filed in each case; designation waives any amount above the small claims limit; a third party that bought or was assigned a claim needs counsel.
rules.consequence: Noncompliance can lead to an order to appear by counsel, costs, default or dismissal.
rules.provider_use: Possible for contract disputes with Indiana fully insured payers without a lawyer. The dollar limit is in the Indiana Code (not read here; see open questions).
rules.quote: cannot be presented or defended by said third party unless this third party is represented by counsel ... as defined by relevant Indiana statutes

rules.applies_to: Benefit claims under ERISA plans (self-funded and insured).
rules.requires: Nothing; it sets where a participant, or a provider standing in the participant's shoes by assignment, may sue for benefits.
rules.consequence: A benefit suit can be filed in state court; whether a provider has standing depends on a valid assignment and the plan's anti-assignment clause (not researched here).
rules.provider_use: After deemed exhaustion (TR-11), a small benefit claim can be filed in state court. Kentucky small claims excludes assigned claims (TR-36).
rules.quote: State courts of competent jurisdiction and district courts of the United States shall have concurrent jurisdiction of actions under paragraphs (1)(B) and (7) of subsection (a) of this section.

rules.applies_to: ERISA plan claims procedures (member benefit claims, including a provider acting as the member's authorized representative). Does not govern the provider's own network contract.
rules.requires: No mandatory binding arbitration of benefit denials; arbitration only as one of the appeal levels and without barring a suit.
rules.consequence: An arbitration clause in a provider contract cannot cut off the member's benefit claim rights.
rules.provider_use: Keep two tracks apart: member-benefit disputes (ERISA procedures, court) and provider-contract rate disputes (contract dispute resolution and arbitration, TR-40 to TR-42).
rules.quote: The claims procedures do not contain any provision for the mandatory arbitration of adverse benefit determinations, except to the extent that the plan or procedures provide that: ... The claimant is not precluded from challenging the decision under section 502(a) of the Act or other applicable law.

rules.citation: 2026 UnitedHealthcare Care Provider Administrative Guide, Chapter 10 (pp. 133-146)
rules.applies_to: UnitedHealthcare contracted providers (commercial, Individual Exchange, Medicare Advantage); the provider's Agreement controls if it differs.
rules.requires: Reconsideration and appeal first, then a Notice of Dispute within 60 days of the appeal decision; bulk reconsideration through the Claims Research Project for 20 or more claims with the same administrative issue.
rules.deadline: Notice of Dispute no later than 60 days after the appeal decision (unless the Agreement differs).
rules.consequence: Missing the Notice of Dispute deadline waives the claim 'in any forum' under the guide's terms.
rules.provider_use: Track the 60-day dispute clock for every UHC appeal decision; use the bulk project for small same-issue items; escalate rate patterns as one Notice of Dispute.
rules.quote: Unless your Agreement prescribes a different time frame, a Notice of Dispute must be sent no later than 60 days after the date of our decision on your appeal. ... Failure to timely comply with this process and the requirements in your Agreement will result in the waiver of your right to initiate dispute resolution and waiver of your right to pursue such claim or issue in any forum. ... If you have a request to reconsider 20 or more paid or denied claims for the same administrative issue (and attachments are not required), you may submit these in bulk online.

rules.citation: Cigna Healthcare, Appeals and Disputes Policy and Procedures (provider site); Cigna Request for Health Care Professional Payment Review form
rules.applies_to: Cigna commercial contracted providers (form at https://static.cigna.com/assets/chcp/pdf/resourceLibrary/medical/RequestForHealthCareProfessionalPaymentReview.pdf).
rules.requires: Arbitration requested within one year of the final internal decision letter; fee-schedule issues across many patients handled without individual appeals.
rules.deadline: One year from the final internal decision letter for arbitration.
rules.consequence: Late arbitration requests are lost; Cigna's own form says multi-patient fee issues need no per-claim appeal.
rules.provider_use: Raise Cigna rate errors once, for all patients, citing the form's own sentence; calendar the one-year arbitration window from the final letter.
rules.quote: With respect to health care provider payment or termination disputes, you must request arbitration within one year of the date of the letter communicating the final internal level review decision. ... Fee schedule or reimbursement terms for multiple patients do not require individual appeals.

rules.citation: MHS (Managed Health Services) Indiana Provider Manual (Jan. 2026), Chapter 5, Arbitration, referring to 405 IAC 1-1.6
rules.applies_to: MHS (Indiana Medicaid managed care), contracted and non-contracted providers; 405 IAC 1-1.6 itself was not read here.
rules.requires: Arbitration after the administrative claim appeal; similar claims may be grouped.
rules.deadline: Postmarked within 60 calendar days of receiving the administrative claim appeal decision.
rules.consequence: Binding arbitration of grouped Indiana Medicaid claim disputes.
rules.provider_use: Group small Indiana Medicaid denials with the same issue into one arbitration request rather than many.
rules.quote: Claims with similar issues from the same provider may be grouped together for the purpose of requesting arbitration. ... The request must be postmarked no later than 60 calendar days after the date the provider received MHS' decision on the administrative claim appeal.

rules.applies_to: The Kentucky Uniform Arbitration Act. Whether a provider participation agreement is an 'insurance contract' was not confirmed; the Federal Arbitration Act may govern payer contracts anyway.
rules.requires: Nothing directly.
rules.consequence: If a court treated a provider agreement as an insurance contract, the state act would not enforce its arbitration clause (the federal act might).
rules.provider_use: Do not rely on this to escape a payer's arbitration clause without a lawyer's opinion; listed so it is not missed.
rules.quote: This chapter does not apply to: ... (2) Insurance contracts.

rules.applies_to: Only qualified IDR items: out-of-network emergency care, out-of-network care at in-network facilities, air ambulance, under group health plans and issuers. Rarely an office dermatology practice's case.
rules.requires: 30 business days of open negotiation, then IDR; batches only for items furnished within the same 30-business-day period and meeting the batching conditions.
rules.consequence: Baseball-style arbitration; the loser pays the IDR entity fee.
rules.provider_use: Only if the practice is out of network at an in-network facility (for example a dermatopathology read for a hospital case); otherwise not a channel.
rules.quote: a certified IDR entity may consider up to 50 qualified IDR items and services jointly as part of a single payment determination

rules.citation: Estate of Lokken v. UnitedHealth Group, Inc., No. 0:23-cv-03514-JRT (D. Minn.), Memorandum Opinion and Order of Feb. 13, 2025 (Doc. 91); Order on Motion to Compel of Mar. 9, 2026 (Doc. 162)
rules.applies_to: UnitedHealthcare Medicare Advantage (members' class action over the nH Predict tool; providers are not parties). A district court ruling, persuasive only.
rules.requires: Nothing of providers. The court waived exhaustion on futility grounds, held most state claims preempted by the Medicare Act, and let contract and good-faith claims proceed because they turn on the plan's own Evidence of Coverage promise that clinicians and physicians decide. In March 2026 the magistrate judge ordered production of documents analyzing nH Predict (not its source data or code).
rules.consequence: Plan documents promising physician decisions are enforceable terms even in Medicare Advantage.
rules.provider_use: Quote the payer's own Evidence of Coverage or provider manual sentence that physicians or clinical staff make decisions, and ask which physician made this one. Do not offer to share information with the plaintiffs in exchange for payment (see TR-48).
rules.quote: Plaintiffs' claims for breach of contract and breach of the implied covenant of good faith and fair dealing, however, survive preemption because those claims do not aim to regulate the same subject matter as the federal standards. ... Clinical Services Staff and Physicians make decisions on the health care services you receive based on the appropriateness of care and service and existence of coverage. ... Accordingly, the contract claims are limited to breaches of EOC terms.

rules.citation: Barrows v. Humana, Inc., No. 3:23-cv-00654-RGJ (W.D. Ky.), Memorandum Opinion and Order of Aug. 15, 2025 (DE 82)
rules.applies_to: Humana Medicare Advantage (members' class action over nH Predict, in Kentucky's federal court; providers are not parties). District court ruling.
rules.requires: Nothing of providers. The court treated Humana's Evidence of Coverage as part of the contract, let contract, good-faith and fraud claims proceed, and dismissed state statutory unfair-claims, unfair-competition, bad-faith and deceptive-practice claims with prejudice as preempted. (The opinion's body and its conclusion differ on the unjust enrichment count.)
rules.consequence: Against Humana MA, state unfair-claims statutes are not a lever; the plan's own written promises are.
rules.provider_use: For Humana MA appeals, cite Humana's own documents (Evidence of Coverage, provider manual) and the federal MA rules, not Kentucky's unfair claims statute.
rules.quote: This Evidence of Coverage is part of our contract with you ... Count 1 (Breach of Contract), Count 2 (Breach of the Implied Covenant of Good Faith and Fair Dealing), Count 3 (Unjust Enrichment), and Count 8 (Common Law Fraud) may proceed ... are DISMISSED with prejudice.

rules.citation: Kisting-Leung v. Cigna Corp., No. 2:23-cv-01477-DAD-CSK (E.D. Cal.), Order Granting in Part and Denying in Part Motion to Dismiss, dated Mar. 30, 2025 (Doc. 55, filed Mar. 31, 2025)
rules.applies_to: Cigna ERISA plan members (class action over the PxDx algorithm; providers are not parties). District court ruling.
rules.requires: Nothing of providers. The benefits claim was dismissed with leave to amend; the fiduciary-duty claim under ERISA 502(a)(3) and the California unfair competition claim survived for some plaintiffs.
rules.consequence: Plan terms promising medical-director review are actionable under ERISA when an algorithm substitutes.
rules.provider_use: In Cigna ERISA appeals, quote the plan's medical-necessity review language and ask who performed the review (pairs with TR-20).
rules.quote: Defendants' motion to dismiss plaintiffs' 29 U.S.C. § 1132(a)(1)(B) claim is granted with leave to amend; ... PxDx algorithm contradicts plan terms promising medical necessity review by a medical director

rules.applies_to: Anyone in Kentucky, including a practice and its staff writing to payers.
rules.requires: No obtaining property by threatening to accuse of a crime, expose a secret harming business repute, bring a boycott, or give or withhold information in another's legal claim.
rules.consequence: Theft by extortion: Class B misdemeanor; Class D felony at $1,000 to under $10,000; Class C felony at $10,000 or more.
rules.provider_use: A demand for payment for services rendered that states the lawful next steps for that same claim (appeal, regulator complaint, external review, lawsuit) is not among the listed threats; and where an accusation or exposure is tied to the same claim, the statute's own defense covers money claimed as compensation for lawful services. Never: threaten criminal charges, threaten a coordinated boycott by practices, or offer to give or withhold information in someone else's lawsuit (for example the class actions in TR-45 to TR-47) to get paid; the defense does not reach (1)(e) or (1)(f). Have a lawyer approve the standard escalation paragraph once.
rules.quote: Accuse anyone of a criminal offense; or ... Bring about or continue a strike, boycott, or other collective unofficial action ... Testify or provide information or withhold testimony or information with respect to another's legal claim or defense. ... It is a defense to prosecution based on subsection (1)(b), (c), or (d) that the property obtained by threat of accusation, exposure, lawsuit, or other invocation of official action was claimed as restitution or indemnification for harm done in the circumstances to which accusation, exposure, lawsuit, or other official action relates, or as compensation for property or lawful services.

rules.citation: IC 35-45-2-1(a)(1), (c)(6) (intimidation), as quoted in Hochstetler v. State, No. 22A-CR-02154 (Ind. Ct. App. July 31, 2023)
rules.applies_to: Anyone in Indiana (applies to communications aimed at Indiana payers).
rules.requires: No communicating a threat with intent that another engage in conduct against its will; 'threat' includes an intention to expose the person threatened to hatred, contempt, disgrace or ridicule.
rules.consequence: Criminal intimidation (penalty levels not read here).
rules.provider_use: Do not threaten publicity (press, social media, reviews) to force payment from Indiana payers. No claim-of-right defense like Kentucky's was found in the quoted text. Full statute text not read (open question).
rules.quote: an expression, by words or action, of an intention to . . . expose the person threatened ... to hatred, contempt, disgrace, or ridicule

rules.citation: Ky. SCR 3.130(3.4)(f) (Rules of Professional Conduct, as reproduced by the Kentucky Bar Association)
rules.applies_to: Kentucky lawyers, including a lawyer who signs or sends the practice's letters.
rules.requires: No presenting or threatening criminal or disciplinary charges solely to gain an advantage in a civil matter.
rules.consequence: Professional discipline of the lawyer.
rules.provider_use: Letters under a lawyer's name must not mention criminal referrals or licensing-board complaints against payer reviewers as leverage.
rules.quote: Present, participate in presenting, or threaten to present criminal or disciplinary charges solely to obtain an advantage in any civil or criminal matter.

rules.applies_to: Every payer, public or private, including self-funded plans: all are 'health care benefit programs'.
rules.requires: No knowing and willful materially false statement or document in connection with payment for health care.
rules.consequence: Up to 5 years in prison (1035); health care fraud up to 10 years (1347).
rules.provider_use: AI-drafted letters must contain only facts the record supports (dates, codes, amounts, what was sent and when). Verify every citation and fact before sending; never assert that records were attached or received when they were not.
rules.quote: makes any materially false, fictitious, or fraudulent statements or representations, or makes or uses any materially false writing or document knowing the same to contain any materially false, fictitious, or fraudulent statement or entry, ... any public or private plan or contract, affecting commerce, under which any medical benefit, item, or service is provided to any individual

rules.applies_to: Anyone presenting a claim or supporting statement to an insurer in Kentucky.
rules.requires: No knowingly false, incomplete or misleading material statement in support of a claim, with intent to defraud or deceive.
rules.consequence: Fraudulent insurance act: Class A misdemeanor; felony from $500 aggregate up.
rules.provider_use: Same discipline as TR-51 under state law; Kentucky also makes licensed practitioners mandatory reporters of suspected insurance fraud (KRS 304.47-050(2)(a)).
rules.quote: knowing that the statement contains any false, incomplete, or misleading information concerning any fact or thing material to a claim;

rules.citation: CMS Medicare Program Integrity Manual (Pub. 100-08), Chapter 3, Section 3.3.2.5 (Rev. 12633, effective June 10, 2024)
rules.applies_to: Traditional Medicare reviewers (MACs, CERT, RACs, SMRC, UPICs); a sound standard for every payer.
rules.requires: Documentation made at the time of service; any later amendment dated, attributed and clearly marked.
rules.consequence: Undisclosed after-the-fact changes are treated as potentially fraudulent and referred to the program integrity contractor.
rules.provider_use: Appeal packets must use the note as signed; AI may summarize a note but must never add clinical facts. Any addendum must be a dated, signed late entry by the clinician.
rules.quote: The date and author of any amendment, correction or delayed entry should be identifiable, and the change/addenda should be clearly and permanently denoted. ... If the MACs, CERT, SMRC or RACs identify medical documentation with potentially fraudulent entries, the reviewers shall refer the cases to the UPIC

rules.applies_to: Providers submitting claims to Indiana accident and sickness insurers and HMOs (not Medicaid).
rules.requires: A person must review any claim before an automated process, system or AI tool submits it.
rules.consequence: Statutory violation (enforcement mechanism not stated in the chapter).
rules.provider_use: Keep a named person's approval on every corrected or resubmitted claim RemitWatch prepares for Indiana payers; the house rule that AI waits for a person meets this.
rules.quote: A provider may not use an automated: ... to submit a health benefits claim without the review of a provider or other person involved in the development of the claim for submission.

rules.applies_to: Funds received under Medicare (title XVIII) or Medicaid (title XIX) by providers, suppliers, Medicaid MCOs and MA organizations; 42 CFR 401.305 is CMS's Medicare rule for it. Whether payments from an MA plan to a provider are covered was not confirmed.
rules.requires: Report and return an identified overpayment within 60 days, or within 180 days while a timely good-faith investigation of related overpayments runs; 6-year lookback.
rules.deadline: 60 days after identification (up to 180 days during a good-faith investigation).
rules.consequence: A retained overpayment becomes an obligation under the False Claims Act (31 U.S.C. 3729).
rules.provider_use: 'Every dollar accounted for' runs both ways: when the same review finds Medicare or Medicaid credit balances or duplicate payments, refund them on the clock. One-sided chasing creates False Claims Act exposure that would hand payers real leverage.
rules.quote: the date which is 60 days after the date on which the overpayment was identified; or ... Any overpayment retained by a person after the deadline for reporting and returning the overpayment under paragraph (2) is an obligation ... The date that is 180 days after the date on which the initial identified overpayment was identified. ... within 6 years of the date the overpayment was received.

rules.citation: 45 CFR 164.506(c)(1); 45 CFR 164.502(b)(1); 45 CFR 164.402 (definition of breach, paragraph (2))
rules.applies_to: The practice as a HIPAA covered entity, for every fax, portal upload and letter to payers and regulators.
rules.requires: Disclosures to obtain payment are permitted but limited to the minimum necessary; a fax to the wrong number is presumed a breach unless a risk assessment shows low probability of compromise.
rules.consequence: Breach notification duties and OCR enforcement for misdirected or over-broad disclosures.
rules.provider_use: Bulk faxing is lawful if each packet carries only what that dispute needs, fax numbers come from the payer's current manual, and transmission confirmations are kept. Pattern letters and regulator complaints should use aggregates, not other patients' identifiers.
rules.quote: A covered entity may use or disclose protected health information for its own treatment, payment, or health care operations. ... a covered entity or business associate must make reasonable efforts to limit protected health information to the minimum necessary to accomplish the intended purpose of the use, disclosure, or request. ... is presumed to be a breach unless the covered entity or business associate, as applicable, demonstrates that there is a low probability that the protected health information has been compromised

rules.citation: 47 U.S.C. 227(a)(5), (b)(1)(C) (Telephone Consumer Protection Act, fax provisions)
rules.applies_to: Fax senders.
rules.requires: No unsolicited fax advertisements (with narrow exceptions).
rules.consequence: Not engaged by appeals, disputes, records responses or complaints, which advertise nothing.
rules.provider_use: High-volume faxing of appeals and disputes is not 'junk fax'. Keep marketing content out of dispute faxes.
rules.quote: The term "unsolicited advertisement" means any material advertising the commercial availability or quality of any property, goods, or services which is transmitted to any person without that person's prior express invitation or permission, in writing or otherwise.

rules.applies_to: Anyone communicating in Kentucky.
rules.requires: Harassing communications need intent to harass and a communication with no legitimate purpose.
rules.consequence: Class B misdemeanor.
rules.provider_use: Appeals and disputes have a legitimate purpose. Avoid sending identical packets repeatedly with no new content or deadline reason; follow-ups should cite the date sent and the clock that has run.
rules.quote: with intent to intimidate, harass, annoy, or alarm another person ... in a manner which causes annoyance or alarm and serves no purpose of legitimate communication;

rules.applies_to: Kentucky admitted insurers (special investigations units) and the reporting duty of insurers and licensed practitioners.
rules.requires: Insurers keep fraud investigation units and must report suspected fraudulent insurance acts to the Division of Insurance Fraud Investigation.
rules.consequence: Inaccurate or inconsistent submissions at volume can trigger special investigations unit review and a state referral.
rules.provider_use: The real risk of aggressive volume is not the appeals themselves but errors in them; consistent, accurate, documented packets are the defense. No source was found that treats appeal volume alone as an audit trigger.
rules.quote: Every insurer admitted to do business in the Commonwealth shall maintain effective procedures and resources to deter and investigate fraudulent insurance acts prohibited by this subtitle, including a unit that will investigate suspected fraudulent insurance acts. ... Any insurer, agent, or other person licensed under this chapter;

rules.applies_to: Medicare Advantage coordinated care plans and their contracted physicians.
rules.requires: Written notice of reasons and of the right to a hearing before a mostly-peer panel when suspending or terminating a physician; 60 days' notice for termination without cause.
rules.consequence: MA plans can end a contract without cause on 60 days' notice; a termination for a stated reason gets a hearing.
rules.provider_use: Network termination is the main business risk of an adversarial posture; keep letters factual and rule-based so any stated reason would be hard to justify. If terminated, demand the reasons, profiling data and hearing.
rules.quote: The reasons for the action, including, if relevant, the standards and profiling data used to evaluate the physician and the numbers and mix of physicians needed by the MA organization. ... The MA organization must ensure that the majority of the hearing panel members are peers of the affected physician. ... An MA organization and a contracting provider must provide at least 60 days written notice to each other before terminating the contract without cause.

rules.applies_to: Medicare Advantage plans.
rules.requires: No punitive action against a physician for requesting or supporting expedited decisions; no gag on advising or advocating for patients about their care.
rules.consequence: Violations of 422.206 expose the plan to intermediate sanctions.
rules.provider_use: Protection is narrow: it covers expedited requests and patient advocacy, not routine payment disputes. Do not tell the owner that appeals are legally protected from retaliation in MA generally.
rules.quote: An MA organization may not take or threaten to take any punitive action against a physician acting on behalf or in support of an enrollee in requesting an expedited determination. ... An MA organization may not take or threaten to take any punitive action against a physician acting on behalf or in support of an enrollee in requesting an expedited reconsideration. ... An MA organization may not prohibit or otherwise restrict a health care professional, acting within the lawful scope of practice, from advising, or advocating on behalf of, an individual who is a patient and enrolled under an MA plan about

rules.applies_to: Medicaid managed care plans in Kentucky and Indiana.
rules.requires: No punitive action against a provider who supports an enrollee's appeal or requests expedited resolution.
rules.consequence: Enforced through the state Medicaid contract and federal oversight.
rules.provider_use: The broadest federal anti-retaliation protection found: it covers supporting any enrollee appeal. It does not cover the provider's own payment disputes.
rules.quote: The MCO, PIHP, or PAHP must ensure that punitive action is not taken against a provider who requests an expedited resolution or supports an enrollee's appeal.

rules.applies_to: Kentucky managed care plans.
rules.requires: No penalty or termination for discussing medically necessary care with an enrollee or someone acting for the enrollee.
rules.consequence: Contract terms to the contrary conflict with statute.
rules.provider_use: An anti-gag rule, not a shield for payment disputes; no Kentucky statute was found that bars a payer from terminating a provider without cause for filing appeals or complaints.
rules.quote: A health care provider shall not be penalized, or a health care provider's contract with a managed care plan terminated, because the provider discusses medically necessary or appropriate care with an enrollee or another person on behalf of an enrollee.

rules.applies_to: Indiana preferred provider insurers and HMOs (anti-gag); covered individuals filing external grievances.
rules.requires: No penalty for disclosing financial incentives or all treatment options; no retaliation against the patient for external grievances.
rules.consequence: Narrow protections only.
rules.provider_use: Indiana has no general provider anti-retaliation statute for appeals or complaints in the code read; budget for the business risk.
rules.quote: An insurer may not penalize a provider financially or in any other manner for making a disclosure permitted under subsection (a). ... shall not be subject to retaliation for exercising the covered individual's right to an external grievance under this chapter;

rules.citation: 42 U.S.C. 1395ddd(f)(2)(A); 42 U.S.C. 1395kk-1 (former subsection (h) struck by Pub. L. 111-152)
rules.applies_to: Traditional Medicare overpayment determinations against providers.
rules.requires: No recoupment while a timely QIC reconsideration of the overpayment is pending; the old statutory limits on prepayment review no longer exist (CMS manual rules govern).
rules.consequence: Interest accrues if the provider loses; repaid with interest if the provider wins.
rules.provider_use: If Medicare responds to aggressive billing review with an overpayment demand, appealing through reconsideration stops recoupment until decided.
rules.quote: the Secretary may not take any action (or authorize any other person, including any medicare contractor, as defined in subparagraph (C)) to recoup the overpayment until the date the decision on the reconsideration has been rendered. ... struck out subsec. (h) which related to conduct of prepayment review.

batch_and_channel: Kentucky fully insured and Medicaid MCO underpayments: one documented payment-error notice per payer can list every underpaid line; no appeal is required and the insurer must correct within 30 days (KRS 304.17A-708(1)); send within 24 months of the payment (708(2)); no interest accrues on these corrections (806 KAR 17:360 Section 4(4)).

Kentucky late clean claims: interest is owed without any demand (KRS 304.17A-730(2)) and due within 30 days after payment (806 KAR 17:360 Section 4(3)); compute it per claim from the receipt date and list missing interest in a quarterly pattern complaint (fines under KRS 304.99-123).

Indiana fully insured downcodes: one batch appeal for all similar downcodes 'without restriction' and at least 180 days to file (IC 27-1-52-12); every downcode notice must carry CARC and RARC, the reason and criteria, and original and revised codes and amounts (27-1-52-11), which RemitWatch can check automatically.

Indiana fully insured underpayments for 2027 plan years: payment-error notice within 180 days of receiving payment or the right is lost (IC 27-8-5.7-10(d) as amended in 2026); earlier policies two years. Run a weekly batch so nothing ages out.

Kentucky Medicaid MCOs: bundle many claims into one external independent third-party review when a policy or practice is alleged (KRS 205.646(2)); ask for an in-person meeting once claims unpaid 45 days or more exceed $2,500 together (KRS 205.534(1)(b)).
Indiana Medicaid (MHS): group claims with similar issues into one arbitration request, postmarked within 60 days of the administrative appeal decision (MHS provider manual, 405 IAC 1-1.6).

UnitedHealthcare: 20 or more same-issue reconsiderations go in bulk through the Claims Research Project; the Notice of Dispute must follow within 60 days of the appeal decision or the issue is waived (2026 UHC Administrative Guide).
Cigna: fee schedule or reimbursement issues across many patients do not need individual appeals (Cigna payment review form); arbitration within one year of the final internal decision letter.

Traditional Medicare and MA: a party may request reopening of a clerical error at any time (42 CFR 405.980(c)(3); MA via 422.616), which is the cheapest channel for small keying or data errors; third-party payer error is not a clerical error.
